lessons.title: GMAW Equipment and Setup
lessons.body:
Gas Metal Arc Welding (GMAW), often called MIG welding, uses a continuous wire electrode and a shielding gas to join metals. In this lesson, you will learn the basic equipment and how to set it up safely. You need a GMAW power source (welding machine), a wire feeder, a welding gun, a gas cylinder with regulator and flowmeter, and a return lead with clamp. In Africa, common brands include Miller, Lincoln, and local imports like Deca or Telwin. For most small workshops, a 200-amp machine running on 220V single-phase is sufficient for mild steel up to 6mm thick.

Start by placing the gas cylinder upright and secure it with a chain or strap to a trolley or wall. Fit the regulator and flowmeter, then connect the gas hose to the wire feeder. The wire feeder holds a spool of wire (usually 0.8mm or 1.0mm diameter for mild steel). Feed the wire through the drive rolls and into the gun liner. Adjust the drive roll tension so the wire does not slip but also does not crush. Set the wire speed on the machine to a mid-range setting as a starting point.

Connect the work clamp (earth clamp) to your metal workpiece or welding table. Ensure bare metal contactâclean off rust, paint, or oil. The gun tip (contact tip) should match the wire diameter; for 0.8mm wire, use a 0.8mm contact tip. The nozzle (shield cup) directs the shielding gas. Check that the gas flow rate is set to about 10-15 litres per minute (LPM) for indoor welding. Open the gas valve on the cylinder slowly and set the flowmeter.

Before welding, test the wire feed by triggering the gun for a secondâwire should come out smoothly and the gas should flow. Listen for a hiss. If the wire stubs or birds-nests, adjust the drive roll tension or replace the liner. Always wear a welding helmet with at least a shade 10 lens, leather gloves, and a flame-resistant apron. In many African settings, power supply can be unstable; use a voltage stabiliser if possible. Practice on scrap metal first to get comfortable with the controls.

lessons.title: Shielding Gases and Flow Rates
lessons.body:
Shielding gas is critical in GMAW because it protects the molten weld pool from oxygen and nitrogen in the air, which cause porosity and weak welds. The most common gas for mild steel is a mixture of 75% argon and 25% carbon dioxide (often called C25). Pure CO2 is cheaper and gives deeper penetration but more spatter. In Africa, C25 may be expensive or hard to find, so many welders use pure CO2. For stainless steel, use a mixture of 98% argon and 2% oxygen, or tri-mix (helium, argon, CO2). For aluminium, use pure argon.

Flow rate is measured in litres per minute (LPM). Too low a flow rate (below 8 LPM) gives poor shielding, leading to porosity. Too high (above 20 LPM) causes turbulence that draws in air, also causing porosity. For indoor welding, set 10-15 LPM. Outdoors, if there is a breeze, increase to 15-20 LPM and use a windbreak. In dusty or windy African environments, always weld indoors or erect a simple screen from corrugated iron sheets.

To set the flow rate: open the gas cylinder valve slowly, then turn the regulator knob until the float in the flowmeter rises to the desired LPM. Trigger the gun to let gas flow, then adjust again while gas is flowing. After welding, close the cylinder valve and bleed the line. Check for leaks by brushing soapy water on connectionsâbubbles indicate a leak. Replace damaged hoses immediately.

Gas cylinder safety: always store upright, away from heat and sparks. Use a chain to secure. Never weld near a leaking cylinder. In many African workshops, cylinders are exchanged rather than refilled on-site; ensure you get the right gas mix. Keep a spare cylinder if possible. Remember, gas cost is a big part of GMAW, so minimise waste by turning off the gas when not welding for long periods. Use a flowmeter with a clear ball for easy reading.

lessons.title: Wire Electrode Selection and Feed
lessons.body:
The wire electrode in GMAW is a consumable that melts to form the weld. For mild steel, the most common wire is ER70S-6, which has good deoxidizers for welding on slightly rusty or dirty steel. It comes in diameters: 0.6mm, 0.8mm, 1.0mm, and 1.2mm. For thin sheet (1-3mm), use 0.6mm or 0.8mm. For general work (3-6mm), use 0.8mm or 1.0mm. For heavy sections (6mm+), use 1.2mm. In Africa, 0.8mm and 1.0mm are easiest to find. For stainless steel, use ER308L or ER316L. For aluminium, use ER4043 or ER5356.

Wire feed speed (WFS) is measured in metres per minute (m/min) or inches per minute (IPM). It must match your voltage and travel speed. As a starting point for 0.8mm wire on 3mm steel, set WFS around 4-5 m/min (160-200 IPM) and voltage around 18-20V. For 1.0mm wire on 6mm steel, try 6-7 m/min (240-280 IPM) and 22-24V. Always check the wire manufacturer's recommended settings. The wire feeder drive rolls must match wire diameterâuse a groove for the wire size. Tension should be just enough to feed wire without slipping; too tight crushes the wire and causes feeding problems.

The gun liner also must match wire diameter. A worn liner causes erratic feeding. Replace if you see wire shavings or if the wire snags. The contact tip should be replaced when the hole wears ovalâusually after 10-15 kg of wire. Keep the tip clean; spatter can block it. Use anti-spatter spray on the nozzle and tip.

When loading a new spool, cut the wire end cleanly, feed it through the liner, and secure the spool so it doesn't unravel. Do not overtighten the spool hub; it should turn with slight resistance. If the wire birds-nests at the drive rolls, release tension, cut the tangled wire, and re-feed. Store wire in a dry place to prevent rust. In humid African climates, keep spools in a sealed container with silica gel.

lessons.title: Setting Voltage and Wire Speed
lessons.body:
Voltage and wire feed speed (WFS) are the two main controls in GMAW. Voltage controls the arc length and weld bead shape. Wire speed controls the amount of wire fed into the weld, which affects penetration and deposition rate. They must be balanced. If voltage is too low, the wire stubs into the work and spatters; if too high, the arc becomes unstable and the wire may ball up. If wire speed is too low, the arc wanders; if too high, the wire pushes into the work and causes a cold lap.

Start with the machine's recommended settings for your material thickness and wire diameter. For example, for 3mm mild steel with 0.8mm wire, set voltage at 18V and WFS at 4.5 m/min. For 6mm steel with 1.0mm wire, set 22V and 6.5 m/min. These are starting points. Fine-tune by listening to the arc: a steady crackling sound like frying bacon means good settings. A popping or hissing sound means voltage too high or wire speed too low. A stubbing sound means voltage too low or wire speed too high.

To adjust: first set voltage, then adjust wire speed until the arc sounds right. Make test welds on scrap. Look at the bead: it should be smooth, with distinct ripples, and penetrate into the base metal. If the bead is too convex (tall and narrow), increase voltage or reduce wire speed. If too flat and wide, reduce voltage or increase wire speed. For out-of-position welding (vertical or overhead), use slightly lower voltage and wire speed to control the pool.

On many African machines, the voltage is set by a coarse switch (e.g., 1-10) and wire speed by a dial. Note the numbers for future jobs. Keep a notebook. If you change wire diameter or gas mix, re-adjust. Always practice on scrap before welding a critical joint. Remember, machine settings vary with input power; if voltage drops, your settings may need tweaking. Use a voltage stabiliser if possible.

lessons.title: Basic GMAW Beads and Joints
lessons.body:
Now that you have set up your machine, it's time to run beads. A bead is a single pass of weld metal. Start with a flat plate. Clean it with a grinder to bare metal. Set your machine for 3mm steel: 0.8mm wire, 18V, 4.5 m/min WFS, gas at 12 LPM. Hold the gun at a 10-15 degree angle, pushing away from the weld (forehand) or pulling (backhand). For beginners, push angle gives better visibility and gas coverage. Keep the contact tip to work distance (CTWD) at 10-15mm. Too close, the tip overheats; too far, you lose gas shielding.

Trigger the gun and move steadily along the plate. Watch the molten pool. You want a pool about 6-8mm wide. Travel speed should be steadyâtoo fast gives a thin, narrow bead with poor penetration; too slow gives a wide, convex bead with excessive heat. For a 3mm plate, a travel speed of about 20-30 cm/min works. Practice straight beads until you can produce a consistent bead with even ripples. Then try weaving: a slight side-to-side motion to widen the bead. This is useful for filling gaps.

Next, learn joints. The butt joint: two plates edge to edge with a small gap (1-2mm). Tack weld at both ends, then weld from one end to the other. For a square butt on 3mm steel, you can do a single pass. For T-joints: one plate vertical on another. Weld the corner, aiming the wire at the root where the plates meet. Use a 45-degree gun angle. For lap joints: one plate overlapping another. Weld along the edge of the top plate. For corner joints: two plates at 90 degrees, weld the outside corner.

In Africa, common projects include gates, window frames, and vehicle repairs. Practice on scrap of similar thickness. Always tack weld first to prevent distortion. Use clamps or magnets to hold parts. After welding, chip off slag (if any) and inspect. A good bead should be uniform, with no undercut or holes. Clean your welds with a wire brush. Remember, GMAW does not produce slag like stick welding, but spatter can be removed with a chipping hammer or grinder.

lessons.title: GMAW Troubleshooting and Defects
lessons.body:
Even with good setup, problems happen. Learn to recognise defects and fix them. Porosity: small holes in the weld, caused by gas coverage issues. Check for low gas flow, empty cylinder, leaks, or a clogged nozzle. Also, dirty base metal (oil, rust, paint) can cause porosity. Clean with a grinder. If welding outdoors, increase gas flow and use a windbreak. Wire feed problems: if the wire stubs or birds-nests, check drive roll tension, worn liner, or incorrect tip size. Replace worn parts. If the wire slips, increase tension slightly; if it crushes, decrease.

Spatter: excessive spatter can be caused by voltage too high, wire speed too low, or wrong gas mix (pure CO2 gives more spatter than C25). Adjust settings. Use anti-spatter spray. Undercut: a groove melted into the base metal at the weld toe. Caused by voltage too high, travel speed too fast, or gun angle incorrect. Reduce voltage, slow down, or adjust angle. Lack of penetration: the weld does not fuse into the root. Caused by voltage too low, wire speed too high, travel too fast, or joint design too narrow. Increase voltage, reduce wire speed, or open the gap.

Burn-through: holes melted through thin metal. Caused by too much heat (high voltage or slow travel). Use lower voltage, faster travel, or thicker metal. For thin sheet, use 0.6mm wire and lower settings. Distortion: warping due to heat. Use tack welds, weld in short segments, or alternate sides. Clamp parts to a heavy table. Cracks: can occur from poor fit-up, high stress, or wrong wire. Use correct wire for the base metal and ensure good penetration.

In African workshops, power fluctuations can cause inconsistent welds. Use a voltage stabiliser. Keep your machine clean; blow out dust with compressed air. Check cables for damage. Always wear PPE. If a defect appears, cut out the weld and re-weld. Practice on scrap to diagnose. Keep a log of settings that work for different jobs.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: GMAW in African Fabrication Workshops

Gas Metal Arc Welding (GMAW) â commonly called MIG (Metal Inert Gas) welding â is the workhorse process for small and medium fabrication businesses across Africa. Whether you are running a gate and burglar-bar shop in Kumasi, a trailer repair yard in Nairobi's Industrial Area, or a water-tank fabrication unit in Lagos, GMAW gives you higher deposition rates and faster travel speeds than stick (SMAW) welding. That speed translates directly into money: more jobs completed per day, less electrode waste, and cleaner welds that need less grinding before painting or galvanising. This practical reference pulls together the settings, gas data, wire selection logic, and troubleshooting knowledge you need to run GMAW profitably â and to train apprentices who can keep your output consistent.

Why GMAW Matters for African Fabrication Businesses

In most African markets, GMAW becomes economical once you have reliable grid power or a generator capable of running a 200â300 A inverter set. The business case is straightforward:

  • Labour cost per metre drops. GMAW deposition rates of 3â5 kg/hour versus 1â2 kg/hour for SMAW mean a two-man team can finish a security gate frame in half the time.
  • Consumable waste falls. No stub ends. Wire is used almost entirely, and gas costs are predictable per cylinder.
  • Finishing costs fall. Smoother beads reduce grinding and filler for painting or galvanising â critical when you are bidding on municipal or NGO contracts.
  • Skills transfer. Apprentices trained on GMAW can move into higher-value work: stainless steel food equipment, aluminium window frames, and structural steel for poultry houses and greenhouses.

Where grid power is unstable, many workshops pair a 250 A inverter MIG set with a 7â10 kVA generator. Budget for a voltage stabiliser â dirty power destroys control boards and is the single most common cause of premature machine failure reported by welders in Nigeria, Kenya, and Ghana.

Shielding Gas Selection and Flow Rates

Shielding gas protects the molten weld pool from atmospheric oxygen and nitrogen. In Africa, COâ is usually the cheapest and most available option, but it produces a harsher arc and more spatter. Argon-COâ mixes give smoother transfer and are worth the premium for visible or structural work.

Table 1: Common GMAW Shielding Gases for Carbon Steel
Gas / Mix Typical Flow (L/min) Transfer Mode Best For Relative Cost
100% COâ12â18Short-circuit / globularThick plate, general fabricationLowest
75% Ar / 25% COâ14â20Short-circuit / sprayGeneral structural steelMedium

98% Ar / 2% Oâ14â20SprayStainless steelHigh
100% Argon15â22SprayAluminium, non-ferrousHigh

Source: American Welding Society, Welding Handbook, Vol. 2 (9th ed.), and ESAB GMAW Shielding Gas Guide.

Practical African note: Wind is the enemy of gas shielding. In open-air yards â common in Mombasa, Tema, and Durban â build a simple windbreak from corrugated sheet or tarpaulin. If you must weld in wind above ~8 km/h, increase flow to the upper end of the range and use a gas lens nozzle. Never weld outdoors in rain without a shelter; moisture causes porosity that will fail a client's inspection.

Wire Electrode Selection and Feed

Wire diameter drives both your amperage range and your feed speed. Most African workshops standardise on 0.8 mm and 1.0 mm ER70S-6 for carbon steel because it is widely stocked and works on thin sheet through to 8 mm plate.

Source: Lincoln Electric, GMAW Welding Guide (C420.1), and Miller Electric MIG Welding Handbook.

Always match wire to the base metal. For galvanised sheet â very common for roofing and water tanks â use ER70S-6 but grind the zinc back 25 mm from the joint and weld with good ventilation. Zinc fumes cause metal fume fever; see the safety box below.

â  SAFETY WARNING â GMAW FUMES AND UV RADIATION

GMAW produces intense ultraviolet radiation and toxic metal fumes. In African workshops, the three most common â and most dangerous â failures are:

  • No fume extraction when welding galvanised steel. Zinc oxide fumes cause metal fume fever within hours. Weld outdoors, use a fan to blow fumes away from the breathing zone (not across the arc), and wear a P2/P3 respirator.
  • Bare eyes or sunglasses instead of a proper helmet. GMAW UV causes arc eye (photokeratitis) â extremely painful and can cause permanent damage. Use a shade 10â13 auto-darkening helmet.
  • Welding near fuel, paint, or solvent drums. Sparks and spatter travel 10 m or more. Clear the area, and keep a dry powder or COâ extinguisher within reach.

Also check gas cylinder security â a loose COâ or argon cylinder that falls can shear the valve and become a missile. Chain cylinders to a trolley or wall at all times.

Setting Voltage and Wire Speed

On a constant-voltage (CV) GMAW machine, voltage controls arc length and wire feed speed (WFS) controls current. The two are linked: for a given wire diameter, increasing WFS without increasing voltage causes the wire to stub into the plate; increasing voltage without WFS causes a long, unstable arc with excess spatter.

Setting procedure for a new job:

  1. Set voltage from the table for your plate thickness.
  2. Set WFS to roughly the mid-range value.
  3. Run a test bead on scrap of the same thickness.
  4. Listen: a steady "frying bacon" sound means you are close. A harsh crackle means too little voltage; a hiss with spatter means too much.
  5. Adjust WFS up in small increments until the arc is stable, then fine-tune voltage Â±1 V.

Write your successful settings on a card and tape it to the machine. In a busy workshop with multiple operators, this single habit prevents hours of re-tuning and reduces wire and gas waste â both of which come straight out of your margin.

Basic Beads, Joints, and Troubleshooting

For flat and horizontal fillet welds â the bread and butter of gate, tank, and trailer work â use a 10â15Â° push angle with a slight side-to-side weave for wider beads. Keep the contact-tip-to-work distance (CTWD) at 10â15 mm. Too long and you lose shielding; too short and you burn back the tip.

Common defects and their usual causes:

  • Porosity â gas flow too low or too high, wind, dirty base metal, or moisture in the gas line.
  • Spatter â voltage too high, CTWD too long, or wrong gas mix. Anti-spatter spray reduces cleanup time.
  • Lack of fusion â travel speed too fast, current too low, or wrong joint preparation.
  • Burn-through on thin sheet â reduce voltage and WFS, increase travel speed, or switch to 0.8 mm wire.
  • Wire stubbing / bird-nesting â WFS too high for the voltage, kinked liner, or wrong drive-roll tension.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. â Check gas cylinder is chained, regulator set to 12â20 L/min for the job, and no leaks at fittings.
  2. â Confirm polarity is DCEP (electrode positive) for solid wire on carbon steel.
  3. â Match wire diameter and type to base metal thickness and grade.
  4. â Set voltage and WFS from the parameter table, then fine-tune on scrap.
  5. â Clean base metal â grind rust, mill scale, paint, and galvanising 25 mm back from the joint.
  6. â Check CTWD (10â15 mm), torch angle (10â15Â° push), and travel speed.
  7. â Wear shade 10â13 helmet, leather gloves, apron, and P2/P3 respirator for coated steels.
  8. â Clear flammables within 10 m; keep extinguisher within reach.
  9. â Inspect finished weld for porosity, undercut, and lack of fusion before it leaves the bench.

Further Reading

  • Lincoln Electric â GMAW Welding Guide (free PDF)
  • Miller Electric â MIG Welding Handbook & Article Library
  • ESAB â Welding Consumables and Shielding Gas Documentation
  • American Welding Society â Welding Handbook, Vol. 2 (Welding Processes)
  • OSHA â Welding, Cutting, and Brazing Safety Guidance

Prepared for the RISE AFRICA Skills programme â Welding Fundamentals, Module: Gas Metal Arc Welding (GMAW) Fundamentals. Settings are indicative; always verify against your machine manufacturer's data and local material specifications.

quiz.q: What does GMAW stand for?
quiz.explanation: GMAW is the acronym for Gas Metal Arc Welding, also known as MIG welding.

quiz.q: Which component feeds the wire electrode in GMAW?
quiz.explanation: The wire feeder pulls wire from the spool and pushes it through the gun.

quiz.q: What is the typical shielding gas mixture for mild steel GMAW?
quiz.explanation: C25 (75% argon, 25% CO2) is the standard mix for mild steel, balancing penetration and spatter.

quiz.q: What is the recommended gas flow rate for indoor GMAW?
quiz.explanation: 10-15 litres per minute provides adequate shielding without turbulence for indoor welding.

quiz.q: Which wire diameter is most suitable for welding 3mm mild steel?
quiz.explanation: 0.8mm wire is a common choice for 3mm steel, offering good control and penetration.

quiz.q: What does WFS stand for in GMAW?
quiz.explanation: WFS stands for Wire Feed Speed, measured in metres per minute or inches per minute.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of the contact tip?
options: B) To transfer welding current to the wire
quiz.explanation: The contact tip conducts electricity to the wire electrode, creating the arc.

quiz.q: Which gas is used for GMAW welding of aluminium?
quiz.explanation: Pure argon is used for aluminium to provide good cleaning action and arc stability.

quiz.q: What causes porosity in a GMAW weld?
quiz.explanation: Porosity is caused by atmospheric gases contaminating the weld pool due to poor shielding.

quiz.q: What is the recommended CTWD for GMAW?
quiz.explanation: A contact tip to work distance of 10-15mm ensures proper arc characteristics and gas coverage.

quiz.q: Which wire is commonly used for mild steel GMAW?
quiz.explanation: ER70S-6 is a standard mild steel wire with deoxidizers for welding on slightly dirty steel.

quiz.q: What should you do if the wire birds-nests at the drive rolls?
quiz.explanation: Birds-nesting indicates improper tension or a liner issue; release tension, cut the tangle, and re-feed.

quiz.q: What is the effect of too low a gas flow rate?
quiz.explanation: Low gas flow allows air to contaminate the weld, causing porosity.

quiz.q: What is the correct storage position for a gas cylinder?
quiz.explanation: Cylinders must be stored upright and secured to prevent falling and damage.

quiz.q: What does a crackling sound like frying bacon indicate?
quiz.explanation: A steady crackling sound indicates the voltage and wire speed are properly balanced.

quiz.q: What is a common cause of undercut?
quiz.explanation: Excessive voltage melts the base metal edges, causing undercut; reduce voltage or increase travel speed.

quiz.q: Which joint involves two plates at 90 degrees welded on the outside corner?
quiz.explanation: A corner joint has two plates at 90 degrees, welded on the outside corner.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of tack welds?
options: B) To hold parts in alignment
quiz.explanation: Tack welds temporarily hold components in place to prevent distortion during welding.

quiz.q: What should you do before welding to ensure good electrical contact?
quiz.explanation: Clean bare metal ensures good electrical contact and prevents arc instability.

quiz.q: What is the recommended shade for a welding helmet lens in GMAW?
quiz.explanation: A shade 10 or higher protects eyes from the intense arc light.

quiz.q: Which defect is characterised by a groove melted into the base metal at the weld toe?
quiz.explanation: Undercut is a groove at the weld toe caused by excessive heat or incorrect technique.

quiz.q: What is the effect of too high a wire feed speed?
options: C) The wire pushes into the work
quiz.explanation: Excessive wire speed pushes the wire into the weld pool, causing cold lap and poor fusion.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a flowmeter?
options: B) To measure gas flow rate
quiz.explanation: A flowmeter measures the rate of shielding gas flow in litres per minute.

quiz.q: Which wire is used for welding stainless steel?
quiz.explanation: ER308L is a common stainless steel wire for GMAW.

quiz.q: What should you do if you suspect a gas leak?
options: B) Brush soapy water on connections
quiz.explanation: Soapy water bubbles indicate a leak; tighten or replace fittings.

quiz.q: What is the main cause of burn-through?
quiz.explanation: Excessive heat from high voltage or slow travel melts through thin metal.

quiz.q: What is the recommended travel speed for a 3mm plate?
quiz.explanation: 20-30 cm/min is a typical travel speed for 3mm steel to achieve good penetration and bead shape.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of anti-spatter spray?
options: B) To prevent spatter sticking to the nozzle
quiz.explanation: Anti-spatter spray prevents molten spatter from adhering to the nozzle and contact tip.

quiz.q: What is the correct drive roll tension?
options: B) Just enough to feed wire without slipping
D) Tight enough to crush the wire
quiz.explanation: Proper tension feeds wire smoothly without deforming it; too tight crushes, too loose slips.

quiz.q: What should you do if you see wire shavings in the liner?
quiz.explanation: Wire shavings indicate a worn liner; replace it to ensure smooth wire feeding.
